questions.title: What is the precise construction of the NF4 quantization bins from the standard normal quantiles?
questions.question_body: The paper describes NFk (and NF4) as computing the "$2^k+1$ quantiles of a theoretical $N(0,1)$ distribution" and then averaging adjacent quantiles to get the representative values $q_i$. I'm confused about the exact steps: (1) Do we compute $Q_X\left(\frac{i}{2^k+1}\right)$ for $i=0\ldots 2^k+1$ and then take midpoints to get $2^k$ bin centers? (2) How do you handle the asymmetric construction (negative part with $2^{k-1}$ bins and positive with $2^{k-1}+1$) in formulaic detail? (3) Is there an explicit formula or pseudo-code for generating the NF4 lookup table from the standard normal CDF/inverse CDF?

questions.title: Why is NF4 said to be "information-theoretically optimal" for normally distributed weights?
questions.question_body: The authors claim NFk is information-theoretically optimal for zero-centered normal distributions. I understand quantile quantization equalizes occupancy across bins, but can someone explain more formally why quantile/bin-equalization is optimal in the information-theoretic sense for that distribution? Which objective (e.g., minimizing expected squared error, maximizing mutual information) is being optimized, and under what assumptions does equal-occupancy become optimal?

questions.title: How exactly is the scale (quantization constant) computed for NF4 and applied to arbitrary-weight tensors?
questions.question_body: The paper says we rescale a weight tensor into the range $[-1,1]$ via absolute maximum rescaling to match the NF data type range. Is the per-block quantization constant $c$ computed as $c = \frac{127}{\text{absmax}(W^{\text{FP32}})}$ as in the Int8 example, or is it a different mapping for NF4? More concretely: given a block of weights $W_b$, what is the formula for $c_b$ and the forward quantization map from $W_b$ to the stored NF4 codes?

questions.title: Why does NF4 need an explicit zero representable value and how is that implemented?
questions.question_body: The text mentions symmetric k-bit quantization lacks an exact representation of zero, so they construct an asymmetric data type with two sets of quantiles and then remove a duplicate zero. I don't fully get why a discrete zero is important for neural network weights and padding, and how the asymmetric construction ensures a discrete zero while keeping equal expected bin counts. Can someone clarify the mechanism and tradeoffs?

questions.title: What is Double Quantization (DQ) mathematically and how does doubleDequant recover the BF16 weights?
questions.question_body: Double Quantization is described as quantizing the quantization constants $c_2^{\text{FP32}}$ into an FP8 $c_2^{\text{k-bit}}$ and a second-level constant $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$. I'm confused about the algebraic steps: if we store $W^{\text{k-bit}}$ and $c_2^{\text{k-bit}}$ plus $c_1^{\text{FP32}}$, what exact formula recovers $W^{\text{BF16}}$? The paper gives doubleDequant(c1, c2, W) = dequant(dequant(c1, c2), W). Could you expand this to show the numeric operations and the final expression (e.g., $W^{\text{BF16}} = W^{\text{k-bit}} / (c_2\times c_1)$ or similar)?

questions.title: Why subtract the mean from the positive quantization constants $c_2$ before quantizing them?
questions.question_body: The authors say the $c_2^{\text{FP32}}$ are positive and they subtract the mean before quantizing to center them for symmetric quantization. Why is subtracting the mean necessary or helpful here? Does this reduce bias introduced by FP8 symmetric quantization, and how is the mean accounted for during dequantization so that final weights are correct?

questions.title: How does backpropagation work through the quantized weights if the quantized base model is frozen?
questions.question_body: QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained model into LoRA adapters. If the base weights $W$ are frozen, why do we need to dequantize $W$ during the backward pass? Specifically, how are gradients computed w.r.t. LoRA parameters without computing or storing $\partial E/\partial W$? What intermediate derivatives are required and how are they computed with dequantized values?

questions.title: Why does computing $\partial E / \partial L_i$ require dequantizing $W$ to BF16?
questions.question_body: The paper states that while we don't need $\partial E/\partial W$ for updates, computing $\partial E/\partial L_i$ "entails the calculation of $\partial X/\partial W$" and thus dequantization is done in BF16. Can you show the chain of derivatives that leads from the loss to the LoRA parameters and indicate where $W$ appears so that dequantized precision is necessary?

questions.title: What performance or numerical issues arise if we used FP4 instead of NF4 for QLoRA?
questions.question_body: The experiments show NF4 outperforms FP4 and Int4. From a numerical standpoint, why does FP4 fail more often? Is the problem primarily due to poor coverage of the normal weight distribution, outlier sensitivity, or inability to represent zero accurately? Are there examples of failure modes when using FP4 in training/finetuning?

questions.title: How do block size choices (e.g., 64 for weights vs 256 for c2) affect quantization error and memory?
questions.question_body: The authors use a blocksize of 64 for $W$ and 256 for $c_2$. I want to understand the tradeoff quantitatively: how does increasing blocksize change expected quantization error for NF4, and how do these block sizes translate to "bits per parameter" memory overhead (showing the arithmetic)? Why is 64 a good compromise for weights but 256 acceptable for constants?

questions.title: Is the 0.373 bits per parameter memory savings from double quantization computed correctly?
questions.question_body: The paper states that using blocksize 64, double quantization reduces memory from $32/64=0.5$ bits per parameter to $8/64 + 32/(64\cdot256)=0.127$ bits, a reduction of 0.373 bits/parameter. I'm confused about the derivation: where do these fractions come from and why is the original $32/64$ interpreted as 0.5 bits per parameter? Please show step-by-step how each term corresponds to stored bytes and how they map to bits per parameter.

questions.title: How exactly is the dequantization ordering implemented in doubleDequant to avoid numerical instability?
questions.question_body: doubleDequant is dequant(dequant(c1, c2), W). In practice, quantizing constants and then dequantizing back could introduce rounding errors. Is there a recommended order of operations (e.g., multiply by c1 then divide by c2, or vice versa) or use of higher precision temporaries to minimize numeric drift? Are there stability tricks used in the CUDA kernels?

questions.title: Can we get a concrete example (numeric) of quantizing one block using NF4 and double quantization?
questions.question_body: I learn best from worked examples. Could someone show a small numeric example: take a toy FP32 block of 4 numbers, show computing its block absmax or std-based scaling, mapping to NF4 codes (with the NF4 lookup table), storing quantized $W$, compute the per-block $c_2^{\text{FP32}}$, then show how $c_2$ is quantized to FP8 and $c_1$ computed, and finally show dequant to BF16 recovering approximate weights?

questions.title: How do Paged Optimizers interact with PyTorch autograd and gradient checkpointing?
questions.question_body: Paged Optimizers use NVIDIA unified memory to page optimizer states to CPU when GPU memory is low. I'm unclear how this integrates with PyTorch's autograd and gradient checkpointing. If optimizer states are paged out during forward/backward and paged in only at update time, does autograd ever need access to optimizer tensors during backward? Could paging cause race conditions or extra GPU<->CPU copies that block the backward pipeline?

questions.title: Why do the authors recommend placing LoRA adapters on all linear layers rather than only attention projections?
questions.question_body: The paper says that default LoRA (applied to query and value projections only) fails to match full finetuning, and that applying adapters to every linear layer recovers performance. Intuitively, why do other linear layers (e.g., FFN projections, output heads) matter so much for instruction-following adaptation? Is there an explanation in terms of representational capacity or gradient flow?

questions.title: How do you choose LoRA rank $r$ and scalar $s$ when doing QLoRA, and why do the authors say $r$ is not critical?
questions.question_body: The LoRA formula uses $L_1 \\in \mathbb{R}^{h\times r}$ and $L_2 \\in \mathbb{R}^{r\times o}$ and a scalar $s$. The paper claims $r$ doesn't affect performance much in their ablations. How should one choose $r$ and $s$ in practice for different model sizes (7B vs 65B) and datasets? Are there diminishing returns beyond a certain $r$?

questions.title: What is the runtime overhead of dequantizing to BF16 every forward/backward compared to keeping parameters in 16-bit?
questions.question_body: QLoRA stores weights in 4-bit but dequantizes to BF16 for computation. I want to compare pure 16-bit training (weights stored in BF16 throughout) vs QLoRA: does the dequantization step cause extra compute or memory bandwidth that slows training? Are there measured per-step or per-token throughput differences reported in the paper or supplementary?

questions.title: How does QLoRA avoid computing or storing gradients for the base weights $W$ during backward pass in the CUDA kernels?
questions.question_body: Even though $W$ is dequantized for computation, the authors say only LoRA parameter gradients are needed. On the CUDA/kernel side, how is the backward implemented to prevent allocation of huge gradient tensors for $W$? Is there a custom backward that blocks gradient accumulation for $W$ or a trick to set requires_grad=False while still enabling autograd to flow into LoRA?

questions.title: Why did the authors choose BF16 as the computation dtype instead of FP16 or FP32?
questions.question_body: The paper says they dequantize to BF16 and perform matrix multiplication in 16-bit BrainFloat. Why is BF16 preferred in this setting? Is it for dynamic range/stability reasons compared to FP16, or for hardware support on target GPUs? Would training work similarly with FP16 compute or would there be numeric degradation?

questions.title: How reliable are GPT-4-based automated evaluations given the reported order bias and disagreement with humans?
questions.question_body: The authors find a significant ordering effect and only moderate agreement between GPT-4 and human annotators (e.g., Kendall's tau ~0.43, Fleiss kappa small). How should we interpret GPT-4-based relative scores (like percentage of ChatGPT) in light of these biases? Are there practical fixes (e.g., randomized ordering averaging) that make GPT-4 evaluation more trustworthy?

questions.title: What causes the observed mismatch between MMLU performance and Vicuna chatbot performance?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that models tuned on FLAN v2 do well on MMLU but poorly on Vicuna, while other datasets show the opposite trend. Conceptually, why does strong MMLU performance not imply strong chatbot quality? Is this about dataset distribution (multi-choice vs open response), conversational formatting, or reward alignment aspects?

questions.title: How would one reproduce the 65B Guanaco training setup on a single 48GB GPU — what are the critical hyperparameters and steps?
questions.question_body: The abstract claims finetuning a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU in 24 hours. For reproducibility, can someone provide a concise checklist: model checkpoint used (LLaMA 65B), LoRA config (which layers, $r$, $s$), NF4 blocksize, DQ blocksize, optimizer type and hyperparameters (LR, batch size, total steps/epochs), and whether gradient accumulation / paging settings are necessary? I'm especially unsure about batch size vs learning rate scaling for 65B mentioned in the paper.

questions.title: Are there any theoretical limits to how low precision we can go for the base model and still recover performance with LoRA (e.g., 3-bit or ternary)?
questions.question_body: The paper hints that even more aggressive quantization (like 3-bit) combined with LoRA might be possible. From a theoretical or empirical standpoint, what factors limit lowering bit-widths further: distributional mismatch, inability to dequantize precisely enough for gradients into adapters, optimizer noise, or hardware limitations? Is there known work on gradient flow through extremely low-bit weights?

questions.title: How does NF4 compare to quantile-based data types when weights deviate from Gaussianity (e.g., layers with skewed or heavy-tailed distributions)?
questions.question_body: NF4 assumes weights are approximately zero-centered normal. But some layers (e.g., embeddings or final linear layers) might have non-normal distributions or outliers. How sensitive is NF4 to such deviations, and are there heuristics to detect when NF4 will perform poorly vs fall back to true quantile quantization?

questions.title: How are LoRA input gradients memory footprints computed and why are they so dominant compared to LoRA parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper claims for a 7B LLaMA with batch size 1 the LoRA input gradients take 567 MB while LoRA parameters are only 26 MB, and gradient checkpointing reduces input gradients to 18 MB per sequence. Can someone show the formula or steps for computing these gradient memory footprints (e.g., shapes, bytes per element) and explain why input gradients dominate memory in PEFT?
